slides.title: Distance on the Coordinate Plane
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say one line and nothing else yet: “Today the triangle is drawn on a grid, and its legs come from the coordinates.”

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is Notes I's rule before it is written down: same x, so subtract the y's — and 5 − (−3) is 8, across zero. Count the squares on a grid after the reveal if any board says 2. Two minutes silent, then reveal.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Read each word and its meaning once; the notes use them next. Students copy the words, not the definitions.

slides.title: Notes
slides.sub: Copy the rule and the example.
slides.note:
Same y: the points are on one horizontal line, and the distance is the difference of the x's, 5 − (−4) = 9 — or, in pieces, 4 to the axis and 5 past it. Never 1: subtracting 5 − 4 ignores that −4 is on the other side of zero, the state's named misconception ((−2, 0) to (3, 0) is 5, not 1). Same x: the y's, the same way. A distance is never negative.
OFF: 'Across zero, the two pieces add.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
(3, 2) to (6, 6) is on no single line. Draw down from one point and across from the other: the dashed legs meet at (6, 2), a square corner. Across 3, up 4; the segment is the hypotenuse, 9 + 16 = 25, 5. No new formula — the triangle is the method.
OFF: 'Slanted? Draw the triangle. Across, then up.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
(−3, 4) to (2, −2): across from −3 to 2 is 5, down from 4 to −2 is 6 — both across zero, both by subtracting. 25 + 36 = 61, and 61 is not a perfect square: √61 ≈ 7.8 units. The legs can be read off the coordinates without counting.
OFF: 'Across: the x's. Up or down: the y's. Then the theorem.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask what the two points share before anyone subtracts: the x, so the distance is in the y's.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Same x, so the y's: 7 − (−2) = 9 — 2 below the axis and 7 above it. A board with 5 subtracted 7 − 2.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Same y: 8 − (−3) = 11 — a board with 5 subtracted 8 − 3.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Ask whether the points share an x or a y: neither — so draw the right triangle first.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Across 4 − (−2) = 6, up 9 − 1 = 8; 36 + 64 = 100, so 10 units — whole, because 6, 8, 10 is a triple. A board with 14 added the legs.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Across 2 − (−5) = 7, up 1 − (−3) = 4; 49 + 16 = 65 and √65 ≈ 8.06, so 8.1 — a board with 11 added the legs.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).
